761.quote_or_event: “As a universal monarch with his fourfold army and great power, the possessor of the fourteen attributes of a king, (has no equal), neither has a very learned monk.”
761.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana takes the cakravartin, whose fourfold army is the sign of his unmatched power, and uses him as a measure for the learned monk.
761.tie_back: The 'fourfold army' is the same four-limbed force (elephants, chariots, horse, foot) that the Kural calls complete in its parts and ranks first among a king's treasures, though the Jain verse in the end prizes the monk above the monarch.
761.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
761._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The fourfold army matches 'complete in its limbs' closely, but the verse uses royal power only as a simile for spiritual excellence; Jainism does not treat an army as the highest treasure.

762.quote_or_event: “So a novice, who as yet has not suffered pains and is not yet used to a mendicant's life, believes himself a hero till he practises austerities.”
762.explanation: The Sutrakritanga sets the untried novice against the seasoned ascetic: only someone long practised in hardship keeps his courage when trouble comes, while the weak 'become disheartened like cowards in the battle' (1.3.1.7).
762.tie_back: The Kural says courage that holds through defeat and losses is found only in a long-established army, and the Jain text likewise finds staying power only in those hardened by long endurance.
762._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Good parallel of seasoned against untried courage, but it is about ascetic endurance rather than a hereditary army.

763.quote_or_event: “A man believes himself a hero as long as he does not behold the foe, as did Śiśupâla (before he beheld) the valorously-fighting, great warrior.”
763.explanation: The verse mocks bravado that lasts only until the real foe appears, and the next verse adds that once the fight begins such men are cut down (1.3.1.2).
763.tie_back: Like the rats whose sea-like roar comes to nothing when the cobra hisses, the boaster's courage collapses the moment he faces true valour.
763._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified). It shares the theme of empty show undone by real strength, but it has no contrast of numbers and no animal image; the verse is a simile for novice monks.

764.quote_or_event: “Though they tempt him with pleasures, and though they should bind him and carry him home, if he does not care for a (worldly) life, they will not captivate him or make him return to domestic life.”
764.explanation: A monk set firmly on the path cannot be won back by pleading relatives, by temptation or even by force; his resolve can be neither bought nor broken.
764.tie_back: The Kural's true army is one that is not broken and cannot be suborned by the enemy, and the Jain monk shows the same incorruptibility under every kind of pressure.
764._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It matches the 'not won over' quality only; the Kural's 'inherited valour' has no Jain counterpart here, and the setting is renunciation, not war.

765.quote_or_event: “Having heard (this) from the venerable men who control themselves and subdue their senses, the virtuous and the learned do not tremble in the hour of death.”
765.explanation: Mahavira's teaching on the two kinds of death says that those trained in self-control meet death calmly and without fear.
765.tie_back: The Kural praises an army that stands firm even when Death himself comes on in fury, and the Jain verse describes the same fearless steadiness before death.
765.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
765._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It matches fearlessness before death, but it misses the Kural's key point of collective unity and has nothing to do with battle.

766.quote_or_event: “Therefore a worthy and wise man should be careful, ceasing from sin and being entirely happy. The virtuous heroes of faith (have chosen) the great road, the right and certain path to perfection.”
766.explanation: Rishabha's sermon to his sons tells the wise man to follow the 'great road' already taken by earlier heroes of faith.
766.tie_back: One of the Kural's four safeguards of an army is walking the excellent path of those who went before, and the Jain verse urges walking the road the heroes of faith have already travelled.
766._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It matches only one of the Kural's four qualities (the predecessors' path), and the heroism it means is spiritual.

767.quote_or_event: “Suffering from insects a great sage remains undisturbed. As an elephant at the head of the battle kills the enemy, so does a hero (in self-control conquer the internal foe).”
767.explanation: In the list of the twenty-two hardships, the monk who stands firm under stinging insects is compared to a war-elephant at the front of the battle. The next verse forbids him to harm even the insects that bite him (2.11).
767.tie_back: The Kural's army meets and takes the full weight of the enemy's vanguard, and the Jain hero stands at the 'head of the battle' and bears the assault, though his enemy is inside him.
767.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
767._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The front-line image is close; the Jain sense is endurance with total non-violence, not fighting another army.

768.quote_or_event: “As a valiant hero bestriding a trained horse, with heralds singing out to his right and left, (has no equal), neither has a very learned monk.”
768.explanation: The verse borrows the splendour of a mounted hero with heralds on either side as a picture of a learned monk's dignity.
768.tie_back: The Kural says an army can win renown by the splendour of its array alone, and the Jain simile likewise treats outward magnificence as something that commands respect.
768.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
768._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi supplies '(has no equal)'). This is a loose match: the display belongs to one hero, not an army's array, and Jainism places little value on outward show.

769.quote_or_event: “A houseless and poor monk who wanders from village to village may become tired of ascetic life: he should bear this trouble.”
769.explanation: Discontent (arati) is one of the twenty-two hardships, and the monk must overcome it and wander on 'perfectly passionless' (2.15).
769.tie_back: The Kural names lasting discontent and want as things that ruin an army. The Jain text also treats discontent as a danger to be overcome, but it accepts poverty instead of curing it.
769.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.14 (cf. 2.15) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
769._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It is a partial match on discontent only; Jainism takes up poverty voluntarily, the reverse of the Kural's concern with ill-supplied troops.

770.quote_or_event: “There is now no Gina, but there is a highly esteemed guide to show the way; now being on the right path, Gautama, be careful all the while!”
770.explanation: Even without a living Jina, the community of seekers depends on a respected guide to lead it along the path.
770.tie_back: The Kural says that however many steadfast soldiers there are, an army cannot stand without worthy leaders, and the Jain verse likewise treats a trusted guide as essential to those on the path.
770.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
770._accuracy_note: Checked against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi's *G*ina rendered as Gina). The parallel on leadership is loose, and Jacobi himself regards this verse as a later addition.
